Place and Date of Judgment:                    Vancouver,
B.C.

November
26, 1990

The plaintiff appeals the
dismissal of his action for damages for defamation.  The trial was before a
judge and jury.  The verdict was pronounced on January 7, 1988.

The defamation was published
in a broadcast by the defendant Bannerman on March 1, 1985, and followed a discussion
of the trial of Ernst Zundel in Toronto, who was convicted on or about February
28, 1985 on a charge of "spreading false news" concerning the Jewish
people.  The plaintiff Christie was counsel for Zundel at that trial.

The plaintiff pleaded that
these words were defamatory:

I
would also urge those of you who have toyed with the idea of the Western Canada
Concept to see who the lawyer of Ernst Zundel is, Doug Christie.  He is on this
program many times.  Mr. Christie will defend himself saying everybody has the
right to a defence.  That doesn't wash in my view.  Everybody does have the
right to a defence.
Doug Christie has aligned himself so many times with
these perverted monsters that he has to be viewed as one himself, in my view.
He has aligned himself constantly with causes that are just beyond
imagination.  They are so close to racism that it is very hard to understand
his motive
.  Ernst Zundel - I couldn't care less who he is.  I regret that
it ever came to Court.  The last thing in the world you want to do is make
these people famous.  They are idiots, public menaces, they don't understand
history.  They can do an enormous disservice, but by overreacting to them what
you will end up doing is making the problem worse because of course they become
heros among the demented souls of the world.

The plaintiff has emphasized
the underlined words in his argument.

The principal defence was
pleaded in this way:

5.   The
words complained of are fair comment made in good faith and without malice upon
a matter of public interest, illustrations of which are as follows:

(a)the
Plaintiff is defence counsel to James Keegstra concerning the criminal charge
of "willfully promoting hatred against an identifiable group, to wit the
Jewish people", which case has generated a great amount of public
notoriety and controversy;

(b)the
Plaintiff is defence counsel to Ernst Zundel concerning a criminal charge of
"spreading false news" concerning the Jewish people, which case has
generated a great amount of public notoriety and controversy;

(c)the
Plaintiff has represented other persons holding extreme right wing views,
including Heinz Koppe, Dr. Gary Botting, and John Ross Taylor;

(d)in
a role other than as counsel, the Plaintiff has associated himself with persons
and organizations holding extreme right wing views which are racist or close to
racist;

(e)the
Plaintiff has publicly stated certain of his own opinions consistent with
extreme right wing views which views are racist or close to racist;

(f)the
Plaintiff is a well known public figure who seeks public exposure on highly
controversial issues and invites, expressly or impliedly, criticism of his
conduct.

Justification was pleaded
but abandoned during the trial.

The jury found that the
words complained of were defamatory of the plaintiff, but were protected by
fair comment.  The jury found that there was no malice on the part of Bannerman
in publishing these words.

The evidence showed that the
plaintiff Christie had defended James Keegstra on a criminal charge of wilfully
promoting hatred against an identifiable group, to wit "the Jewish people,
and had defended Ernst Zundel on a charge of "spreading false views concerning
the Jewish people", and that both proceedings generated a great amount of
public notoriety and controversy.

The preliminary hearing in
the
Keegstra
case and the trial of the
Zundel
case both preceded
Bannerman's broadcast.

Both the plaintiff Christie
and the defendant Bannerman gave evidence at the trial.  Bannerman testified
that his reference to "perverted monsters" was to Keegstra and to
Zundel.

The plaintiff agrees that
the pertinent facts may be taken as stated in the defendants' factum:

(a)the
Appellant defended James Keegstra on a charge of promoting hatred against Jews
and, in particular, was counsel for Keegstra at the preliminary hearing, which
occurred before Bannerman's editorial;

(b)the
Appellant did not seek a ban on publicity at the preliminary hearing, as a
result of instructions from his client;

(c)some
of the students of Keegstra gave evidence at the preliminary hearing that he
had taught them about a Zionist conspiracy, and others said that he had taught
them about a Jewish conspiracy;

(d)it
was "perhaps" said by some of the students that "the Jews are
rich intellectual playboys, money thugs, gutter rats, cutthroats";

(e)the
Appellant did not know if he had said, concerning the Keegstra case, that
"the right to teach or speak of moral values is at stake";

(f)it
is "possible" that the Appellant said, with respect to the Keegstra
case, that it would be "the trial of the last two centuries", because
the year 1776 was the origin of the alleged conspiracy discussed in the case;

(g)the
Appellant also represented Ernst Zundel on a charge of "spreading false
news";

(h)the
case concerned two publications by Zundel, one entitled "Did Six Million
Really Die?".  Zundel alleged the existence of an international conspiracy
of Zionists and Freemasons to manipulate world history and create wars in the
Middle East;

(i)it
would have been a total defence to the charge against Zundel to raise a
reasonable doubt that he honestly believed what he said was true, but the
defence in the case went beyond that and attempted to prove that it was true;

(j)the
reason for this was that it was felt that honest belief would be more readily
accepted if it were also established that the facts were true;

(k)the
Appellant stayed at Zundel's home in Toronto during the trial, which was from
the beginning of January, 1985, until February 28, 1985, because he "could
be secure and safe in one spot", as some people had been hurt during the
trial.

(l)the
Judge during the Zundel trial admonished the Appellant at one point for
apparently saying "we are on trial for spreading false news" (i.e.
identifying himself with his client), but the Appellant says that he in fact
said that "we are on
a
trial for spreading false news".  He
understands that a lawyer should not identify himself with his client;

(m)on
approximately February 28, 1985 (Bannerman's broadcast having been on March 1,
1985) a portion of an interview with the Appellant was shown on the C.B.C. news
program, "The Journal";

(n)on
that program the Appellant said in some context that "I have grave doubts
about the, ah, the way it is presented.  I think the gas chamber story - I just
can't believe it.  I am sorry, I'm an unbeliever, but that's the way it
is".

6.   The
Respondents add the following facts from the evidence of the Appellant's
witness, Richard Lewers:

(a)the
Appellant is an active General Counsel of the Canadian Free Speech League and
advises the Directors of that organization on such matters as making donations
to accused persons in cases involving freedom of speech;

(b)the
Canadian Free Speech League raised money for the defence of both Keegstra and
Zundel.

7.   The
Respondents add the following facts from the evidence of Bannerman:

(a)he
was aware that the Appellant was representing Keegstra and Zundel and he
followed those cases in the media;

(b)he
saw the clip of the Appellant on the C.B.C. news program, "The
Journal" on February 28, 1985, and construed this as "an absolute
declaration" of where the Appellant "stood on the issue";

(c)in
giving his editorial he was motivated by the Appellant's statements on
"The Journal" and by the Zundel trial and "everything else"
he saw;

(d)he
was aware that the Appellant did not seek a ban on publicity at the preliminary
hearing in the Keegstra case and was surprised at that "in the sense of
conducting a case", but was not surprised "if publicity was the
motive";

(e)he
honestly believed that Keegstra and Zundel were "perverted monsters";

(f)he
honestly believed that the Appellant was a "perverted monster"
because he had "crossed the line" and "become an active
participant in this cause";

(g)in
using the term "perverted monsters" he was referring to the
perpetuation of an unhealthy, unnatural, twisted view of the world and the act
of "affecting the minds of children and feeding them lies".

The plaintiff alleges errors
in the conduct of the trial, and errors in the charge to the jury.  The
plaintiff submits:

1
.The
cumulative effect of improper cross-examination of the plaintiff, and
statements by defence counsel during cross-examination and his address to the
jury was prejudicial to the plaintiff.  He submits that his evidence in chief
and upon re-examination was unduly restricted.

2
.There
was misdirection and non-direction on the issue of malice, and on the defence
of fair comment.

The conduct of the trial.

A careful review of the
examination, cross-examination and re-examination of the plaintiff leads me to
conclude that there is no basis for saying that this trial was not conducted
properly.

Most of the evidentiary
questions which the plaintiff now raises are related to a ruling of the trial
judge (to which no objection is taken) that evidence of acts or declarations,
subsequent to the date of Bannerman's broadcast, were not admissible to show
honest belief by Bannerman in what he said on March 1, 1985.  But the judge
made it clear that subsequent events could be relevant on the issue of
damages.  No objection was taken at trial to that proposition.  In keeping with
that ruling there was cross-examination of the plaintiff with respect to an
action against the Edmonton Sun (Transcript, pp. 128-131), and to comments in
the press about an incident in Beacon Hill Park in Victoria.  There was also
cross-examination with respect to an interview given by Christie in l986
concerning the Zundel charges (Transcript, pp. 108-111).

There was a reference in
cross-examination to the conviction of Keegstra on July 25, 1987.  But this was
of no consequence.  The emphasis with respect to the Keegstra charge was on the
plaintiff's tactics at the preliminary hearing (not seeking a ban on
publication) and his statements concerning that proceeding ("This will be
the trial of the last two centuries").

I am not persuaded that the
cross-examination was improper, or that the trial judge failed to keep it
within proper bounds.

The conduct of defence counsel
:

(a)
Cross-examination
.

The plaintiff complains of
one incident.  He was being cross-examined with respect to a letter which the
defendants alleged he had written before the Bannerman broadcast.  It was
entitled "A Message from Doug Christie".  The plaintiff said that he
could not recall it.  Finally, defence counsel said:

Now,
I am alleging that the contents are so outrageous that it cannot be truthful to
say he can't remember.

Christie gave this answer:

Well,
I can tell you I didn't write this.

There was a voir dire, and the letter
was not admitted in evidence.  The jury were left with the evidence that
whatever the letter said that Christie had not written it:  no objection was
taken by counsel for the plaintiff, and the judge was not asked to give any
instruction to the jury concerning this "flare up".  The trial turned
to other matters, and I do not think that the outcome was affected by this
incident, which occurred early in the trial.

(b)
Address to the Jury by
defence counsel.

The address of defence
counsel was directed towards establishing that there was a basis for the belief
of Bannerman that the plaintiff had aligned himself with the interests of his
client Zundel.  After the trial, the plaintiff spoke on national television.
He said he did not believe the gas chamber story.  Defence counsel made this
argument:

I
suggest if there's any way to identify yourself with the very opinion and
statements of your client, that's it.  For a lawyer to say that, one who is
defending a murder case, what would you say?  I'm glad my client shot him?
That's what this is about.

Later defence counsel said:

If
there is any diminishment of his reputation in the community I suggest it's
because what he said on national T.V. was absolutely appalling.  If a lawyer is
looking at them, it is even more appalling to think that you are saying I take
unpopular causes and then get on television and make those kinds of
statements.  From a lawyer's perspective I suggest that is unforgivable.

The plaintiff submits that
to permit defence counsel to express those views was to allow him to give
evidence.  But this was argument, not evidence.  It was strong language, but it
was properly based on the evidence, and was intended to persuade the jury that
Bannerman honestly believed that Christie had aligned himself with his client's
cause.  No objection was taken by plaintiff's counsel.

In my opinion there is no
merit in the plaintiff's submissions that the trial judge failed to conduct a
fair trial.

The charge to the jury
.

The real issue in this trial
was whether the defendant Bannerman had a honest belief in the opinion that he
expressed.

The publication of the
statement was admitted.  The defendants did not seriously dispute that the
words were defamatory.  The judge, while expressing his opinion that the words
were comment rather than a statement of fact, told the jury that they must
decide that issue.  At the request of plaintiff's counsel he redirected the
jury on that issue.

In dealing with the defence
of fair comment the judge directed the jury that the comment must be based on
true facts, that it must be of public interest, and must represent the honest
expression of the real view of the person making the comment.  When a mild
objection to the latter question was made the trial judge said that he had
applied the test proposed by Nemetz C.J.B.C. in
Vander Zalm
v.
Times
Publishers et al

(1980,
1980 CanLII 389 (BC CA)
,
109 D.L.R. (3d) 531
at pp. 535-6
:

The
three elements of the defence of fair comment are well known.  First, the
matter must be recognizable to the ordinary reasonable man as a comment upon
true facts, and not as a bare statement of fact.  Secondly, the matter
commented upon must be one of public interest.  There must, in short, be a public
nexus between the matter and the person caricatured.  In a case such as this,
the cartoonist may not intrude upon the private life of a public man, no matter
how interesting such an intrusion may be to the public, nor may he expose a
private person to unsought publicity.  Finally, as explained by Diplock, J. (as
he then was), in
Silkin v. Beaverbrook Newspapers Ltd. et al.

[1958] 1 W.L.R. 743
at p. 747,
and by
the Supreme Court of Canada in
Cherneskey v. Armadale Publishers Ltd. et al.

(1978),
1978 CanLII 20 (SCC)
,
90 D.L.R. (3d) 321
,
[1979] 1
S.C.R. 1067
, [1978[] 6 W.W.R. 618, the comment must be "fair" in that
it must, to quote Martland, J.,
in

Cherneskey
at p. 325 D.L.R., p. 1073 S.C.R.,
"represent an honest expression of the real view of the person making the
comment"

Counsel for the plaintiff
said he did not quarrel in a substantial way with the direction of the trial
judge but submitted that this direction taken from
Silkin
would have
been appropriate:

Would
a fair-minded man holding strong views, obstinate views, prejudiced views, have
been capable of making this comment?  If the answer to that is yes, then your
verdict in this case should be a verdict for the defendants.  Such a verdict
does not mean that you agree with the comment.  All it means is that you think that
a man might honestly hold those views on those facts.

I agree with the trial judge
that it was unnecessary in this case to give that further direction.  In any
event the failure to do so would not prejudice the plaintiff.

In my view the directions on
the defence of fair comment were correct.

Malice
.

The issue of malice was left
to the jury although there was little evidence of it.  The plaintiff submits
that Bannerman provided evidence of malice when he testified that he found some
of the views of Christie and of the Western Canada Concept, a political
movement with which Christie was associated, "to be quite repugnant to my
way of thinking".  The plaintiff also submits that the defamatory words
were so excessive, grossly exaggerated and intemperate that they constituted
evidence of a state of mind reckless of the consequences and hence malicious or
intending harm to the plaintiff.  The plaintiff submits that the trial judge
erred when he gave these directions to the jury:

Fair
comment will not succeed, even if proved, should you decide the defamatory
statement was published as a result of malice.
Now, mention was made by
counsel that malice is implied by the mere publication of a defamatory
statement
.
That is true but it does not really apply in this case
.
If fair comment is not found, then the Plaintiff succeeds and you will not have
to consider malice.  If fair comment is found by you as members of the jury,
then actual malice must be shown on the part of Bannerman.  Should you find
that the evidence makes you conclude that Bannerman made his statements about
Christie to harm him, that his motive was to destroy him as a politician, or as
a person, or as a lawyer and not to simply give his editorial to inform,
educate and perhaps entertain his listeners, then you might find malice.
On
the other hand, should you find that he honestly believed the comment and made
it in the context of the editorial, then there is no malice
.

(emphasis
added)

The plaintiff submits that
the trial judge not only failed to direct the attention of the jury to the
extrinsic and intrinsic evidence, which might have supported a finding of
malice, but left them with the impression that they should not consider the
content of the publication at all.

I agree that it would be
wrong to tell the jury that they could not have reference to the language used
and the tone of voice of the commentator in considering malice.  Those were
matters they should have considered, together with any other evidence of improper
motive.  There was non-direction on that point.  It was accompanied by
misdirection when the judge told the jury, in effect, that a finding of honest
belief would negate malice.  The two are not to be confused.  Honest belief is
at the root of a successful defence of fair comment.  Malice will defeat fair
comment.

Watt v. Longsdon
,

[1930] 1 K.B. 130
at pp. 154-155
is cited by the plaintiff.  This passage from
the judgment of Greer, L.J. draws the distinction between honest belief and
malice, and emphasizes the importance of the language used in the defamatory
statement:

Malice
is a state of mind:  see the judgments in the case of
Nevill v. Fine
Arts and General Insurance Co., Ld.
(1) in the Court of Appeal.  A man may believe
in the truth of a defamatory statement, and yet when he publishes it be
reckless whether his belief be well founded or not.  His motive for publishing
a libel on a privileged occasion may be an improper one, even though he
believes the statement to be true.  He may be moved by hatred or dislike, or a
desire to injure the subject of the libel, and may be using the occasion for
that purpose, and if he is doing so the publication will be maliciously made,
even though he may believe the defamatory statements to be true.  I agree with the
statement of the law contained in the late Mr. Blake Odgers' monumental book on
libel and slander, which will be found at p. 354 of the 5th edition.  It is as
follows:  "And even though it is clear that the defendant believed in the
truth of the communication he made, and was acting under a sense of duty on a
privileged occasion, the plaintiff may still rely upon the words employed, and
the manner and mode of publication, as evidence of malice.  An angry man may
often be led away into exaggerated or unwarrantable expressions;  or he may
forget where and in whose presence he is speaking, or how and to whom his
writing may be published.  Clearly this is often but faint evidence of malice;
the jury will generally pardon a slight excess of righteous zeal.  In some
cases, however (which we will proceed to examine) such excess has secured the
plaintiff the verdict.  But if the jury find there was no malice in the
defendant, such excess becomes immaterial".

In my opinion there was
non-direction and misdirection on the issue of malice.

Should a new trial be ordered
?

The factors to be considered
are those set forth in
Arland and Arland v. Taylor
,
1955 CanLII 145 (ON CA)
,
[1955] 3 D.L.R. 358
,
a case which was referred to with approval by Hutcheon, J.A., speaking for this
Court, in
Hayes v. Thompson and Bell

(1985),
1985 CanLII 151 (BC CA)
,
60 B.C.L.R. 252
, at pp.
263-4
.  In
Arland
, at pp. 364-5, Laidlaw, J.A. set forth these general
propositions:

(1)  A
new trial is contrary to the interest of the public and should not be ordered
unless the interest of justice plainly require that to be done.

(2)  An
appellant cannot ask for a new trial as a matter of right on a ground of
misdirection or other error in the course of the trial when no objection was
made in respect of the matter at trial.

(3)  A
new trial cannot be granted because of misdirection or other error in the
course of the trial "unless some substantial wrong or miscarriage has been
thereby occasioned".

(4)  A
party should not be granted a new trial on the ground of non-direction in the
Judge's charge to the jury where, having opportunity to do so, he did not ask
the Judge to give the direction the omission of which he complains of.

Arland
was referred
to by the Supreme Court of Canada in
Leslie v. Canadian Press
,
1956 CanLII 23 (SCC)
,
[1956] 5
D.L.R. (2d) 384
at pp. 386-7
.  At p. 387 Kerwin, C.J.C. made this statement
about the onus of proof:

Bearing
in mind the right of the plaintiff in such an action as this to have the issues
passed upon by the jury, I am of opinion that the preferable rule and the one
that should be adopted is that it is sufficient for the complaining party to
show that a misdirection may have affected a verdict and not that it actually
did so;  and that, if an Appeal Court is in doubt as to whether it did or not,
it is then for the opposite party to show that the misdirection did not in fact
affect the verdict.

No objection was taken to
the charge on malice in this case.  Other objections were taken, and resulted
in further directions by the trial judge.

I think that the reason no
objection was taken to the charge on malice was that it was not perceived as a
live issue at the trial.  Counsel for the plaintiff made only this cursory
reference to malice in his address to the jury:

Now,
those fair comments can be defeated if we establish that there was malice in
making the comments.

No evidence was led by the
plaintiff, and no argument was presented to support a finding of malice.

The jury heard a tape of the
broadcast.  They heard the tone of voice of the commentator (which, we are
told, was moderate), and the language used by him.  They heard and saw him give
evidence.  They were told that they might find malice if they concluded that
Bannerman's motive was to harm or destroy Christie as a politician, a person or
as a lawyer, rather than to inform, educate and entertain his listeners.  In my
view there was no basis in the evidence for finding such an improper motive on
the part of Bannerman, and I am satisfied that the non-direction and
misdirection did not affect the verdict.  It would not be in the interests of
justice, there being no substantial wrong or miscarriage, to order a new trial
when the result must inevitably be the same.

I would dismiss the appeal.

"The
Honourable Mr. Justice Macfarlane"

I AGREE:  The Honourable Mr. Justice
Anderson

I AGREE:  The Honourable Mr. Justice
Toy
